transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Veridian), Markus Chen (Head of ML), Sofia Patel (Infra Engineer), Evan Ross (Product Manager)

[00:00] Jared Kim: All right hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off on time. Quick agenda: scope the POC workloads, confirm QPS/concurrency and token distributions, agree success criteria and timeline, and then next steps. Priya and Marco from the eng team will cover the benchmark plan.

[00:15] Lena Ortiz: Thanks Jared, yeah we want to be fairly pragmatic - two main things for us: real-time fraud scoring for transactions (low-latency, high-QPS) and a customer support assistant for dispute handling (higher token counts, lower QPS).

[00:35] Priya Nair: Great, that matches what we saw in the email. Can you share rough traffic numbers now so we can map to concurrency and batching?

[00:45] Markus Chen: Sure. Baseline for scoring is around 30 QPS during business hours, but we have peaks up to 180 QPS for major sale events. Average request size for scoring is small - about 40 input tokens (we include transaction meta) and output is just a short label or explanation, say 12 tokens. For the chat assistant, it's about 6 QPS on average, peaks to 20 during campaign, prompts average 220 tokens, responses ~280 tokens.

[01:10] Marco Alvarez: OK so two very different profiles - scoring is latency-sensitive, chat is throughput/compute-sensitive. For the POC do you want us to prioritize a single SLA or demonstrate both?

[01:25] Lena Ortiz: We need both, but the business decision will hinge on the scoring SLA. If scoring can't meet p95 latency of under 200ms we can't move forward for that use case. Chat is secondary from a timeline perspective.

[01:40] Priya Nair: Understood. A couple of clarifying questions - is scoring called synchronously inline in your transaction path? Are you comfortable with an async fallback?

[01:50] Sofia Patel: For now scoring is inline within our authorizations flow - it must return quickly. We can consider an async fallback for low-confidence cases but the normal path must be sync. Also we have strict egress rules, everything must stay in our VPC or private peering and KMS for key management. No data should leave region.

[02:10] Jared Kim: That's expected for enterprise. We'll note VPC-only requirement and KMS. Our Private offering supports a VPC control plane and HSM/KMS integrations; we'll include that in the security docs.

[02:30] Evan Ross: On evaluation, Markus will supply labels for the scoring model so we can measure precision/recall. We want model quality to hit at least 95% precision on high-risk transactions for the POC.

[02:45] Markus Chen: Right - we'll supply a labeled sample set ~10k transactions with a 1-2% positive class. We'll also include a 7-day traffic dump (anonymized) so you can model sequence length distributions.

[03:05] Priya Nair: Perfect. For benchmarking we'll do: (1) hosted API baseline, (2) Dedicated reserved pool with our recommended batch/quantization config, (3) Dedicated with quant and KV cache enabled. We want steady-state runs and spike tests. Typical bench matrix: 30 minutes steady at target QPS, then 10x burst spikes at 1-minute intervals.

[03:30] Marco Alvarez: For the scoring endpoint, because prompts are short, continuous batching helps but increases p95 if batch windows are long. We'll tune batching to keep p95 under 200ms. We'll present the latency vs cost trade-off in the spreadsheet.

[03:50] Lena Ortiz: Can you give a rough capacity estimate now? If we target sustained 60 QPS with 200 QPS peaks, what hardware should we expect?

[04:05] Priya Nair: Rough back-of-envelope: for a 7B-ish model with F16/INT8 quant, you can serve roughly 60-100 QPS per high-memory GPU for short-token workloads depending on kernel optimizations. With KV cache and optimized kernels on A100 or H100 class, the scoring workload (avg 52 tokens total) would likely need 2-3 GPUs for the sustained 60 QPS with room for burst headroom. If peaks to 200 QPS are frequent, we'd recommend autoscaling or a dedicated pool sized for 200 with burst capacity.

[04:35] Markus Chen: When you say 60-100 QPS per GPU, is that with batching enabled? What's the p95 we should expect?

[04:45] Marco Alvarez: Yes that's with continuous batching tuned for micro-batches (batch sizes 8-16 depending on latency SLO). p95 will vary; for scoring we can expect p95 around 120-220ms on optimized kernels on H100-class with dedicated capacity and KV caching for repeated prefixes. Hosted may be slightly higher due to multi-tenant variability. We'll run concrete numbers in the bench.

[05:10] Evan Ross: And cost implications - we care about unit economics, what's your expected token-cost comparison between hosted and dedicated?

[05:20] Jared Kim: In general, dedicated reduces per-token cost substantially at scale because you amortize GPU and get optimized runtimes and quantization. We'll put an apples-to-apples estimate in the spreadsheet (tokens per second, cost per 1M tokens).

[05:35] Lena Ortiz: For chat assistant - longer tokens - what concurrency do you need to test? We expect 25-30 concurrent sessions during peak.

[05:50] Priya Nair: For chat sessions with ~500 tokens total (prompt+response), throughput is limited by token-generation speed. We'll simulate 30 concurrent sessions with average turn length and a 30-second think time. That map will show cost and latency tradeoffs.

[06:10] Sofia Patel: Important: our infra team needs to validate network load and connection concurrency (SYN/TTL) requirements. We'll share our egress baseline and max open connections.

[06:25] Marco Alvarez: Noted. We'll include connection churn and keepalive settings in the bench. Also we'll test cold-start latency for the model (idle to first token) since that's relevant for cost when scaling down.

[06:40] Markus Chen: On quality gating - we'll need a few evaluation prompts to define regression criteria, and we want Redwood to run a blackbox quality run using our labels to measure precision/recall and false positive rates.

[06:55] Priya Nair: Yes - we'll accept the labeled CSV. We'll run scoring locally in the bench harness and provide confusion matrix and CSV of predictions. Expect an initial run within the first bench report.

[07:10] Lena Ortiz: Timeline question - how soon can Redwood start the benchmarks and when can we expect results?

[07:20] Jared Kim: If we get the traffic sample and labels by next Friday (2026-07-02), we can start bench week of 2026-07-06. A first pass of results (hosted vs dedicated baseline) by 2026-07-10, and the full matrix by 2026-07-16. That fits a two-week POC window with decision by end of July.

[07:40] Evan Ross: Sounds good. Security docs and SOC2 - we need that to route to procurement.

[07:50] Jared Kim: I'll email SOC2 report, architecture notes for VPC/private, and KMS/HSM integration steps. We'll also attach a checklist for legal and procurement.

[08:05] Lena Ortiz: One more ask - Can you show a degradation/fallback policy? For example if Dedicated pool is saturated do you fall back to hosted or a simpler rules-based scoring?

[08:20] Marco Alvarez: Yes, our smart routing supports fallback to regional hosted endpoints or to a lighter-weight model variant. We'll demo the routing and can include a Canary/A-B policy for cutover. We'll include failure modes and RTO estimates in the bench doc.

[08:40] Priya Nair: We'll also include recommended quantization profiles - like INT8 for chat to save cost, mixed precision for scoring to keep latency down. We'll show latency vs token-cost plots per config.

[08:55] Markus Chen: Are there constraints on logging? We need masked logs and PII redaction.

[09:05] Jared Kim: Redwood supports token-level redaction and configurable retention. For Private we can hook into your logging stack so no sensitive logs leave your environment. We'll note that in security docs.

[09:20] Evan Ross: Ok let's recap next steps quickly so procurement and infra have concrete items.

[09:30] Jared Kim: Recap: 1) Veridian provides 7-day sample traffic CSV and labeled eval set by 2026-07-02 (Markus). 2) Redwood runs benchmark matrix (hosted, dedicated, dedicated+quant+KV) starting 2026-07-06 and shares preliminary results 2026-07-10, full by 2026-07-16 (Jared/Priya). 3) Infra deep-dive scheduled (Priya to set up with Sofia by 2026-07-01). 4) Security docs to be shared by Jared today. 5) We'll include a benchmark spreadsheet link and a short demo deck.

[09:55] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. If the scoring SLA and costs look good we'll move to a 30-day pilot with dedicated pool and a committed capacity conversation.

[10:10] Jared Kim: Great thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the sheet and calendar invites. Meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had a few mis-heard technical names, and some speaker labels got swapped in a couple of short exchanges. There is natural crosstalk and filler words preserved.
